articles.title: Genetic scores linked to depression and neuroticism are associated with lower voter turnout
articles.summary: A recent study of over 50,000 individuals reveals that genetic predispositions for health and personality traits predict voter turnout. Using advanced DNA scoring, researchers shed light on how genetics might influence our likelihood to engage in the political process.

articles.title: Musicians are less prone to the ventriloquism illusion, study finds
articles.summary: A flash of light can make a sound seem to come from the wrong place. Musicians are less susceptible to this illusion, a new study suggests, possibly because they are less inclined to assume the two share a source.

articles.title: Creative drawing ability is linked to the brain’s white matter wiring, study finds
articles.summary: People who scored higher on a creative drawing test tended to have stronger white matter in pathways tied to movement and vision, according to a brain imaging study of 142 young adults in Austria.

articles.title: Frontiers: A Roundtable Discussion on the I-Frame vs. S-Frame Debate
articles.summary: Applied behavioral scientists believe their work can influence people’s lives for the better. But what is the most effective way to make that happen? Is it through interventions focused on influencing individual behavior while maintaining freedom of choice? Is it by changing policies and laws, and thereby the systems, that individuals operate within? Is it a combination of the two? Is the distinction between an individual- or systems-focus a helpful one? Or, is the world too messy and complex? How should applied behavioral scientists navigate the financial and political influences on the work

articles.title: Researchers identify a factor linked to how much happier couples are than singles
articles.summary: Partnered people tend to be more satisfied with their lives than singles, but a study of more than 380,000 adults in Great Britain suggests the size of that gap is tied to how common relationships are in the local area.

articles.title: Scientists uncover a possible trade-off in how the hippocampus replays new memories
articles.summary: When the brain rests after learning, it actively replays recent experiences. A new brain imaging study reveals this mental replay prioritizes general themes while stripping away specific details, suggesting false memories are a natural byproduct of learning.

articles.title: Is fatness a feminist issue?
articles.summary: Feminist scholars have long argued that anti-fat stigma is rooted in sexism. But when researchers asked fat women directly, many disagreed, some framing their weight as a personal matter, and a few even said fat women deserve to be teased.

articles.title: Patience with life’s small annoyances is linked to lower anxiety, but it doesn’t buffer spiritual struggles
articles.summary: Spiritual doubts are linked to higher anxiety in college students, but a new study finds that cultivating patience for everyday annoyances—like traffic and long lines—can independently predict a reduction in generalized anxiety over time.

articles.title: Scientists find hidden driver of aging and a simple amino acid that fights memory loss in mice
articles.summary: Scientists discovered that declining levels of a protein called Menin may help drive aging, and restoring it in older mice reversed several age-related changes in just 30 days. Even more surprisingly, supplementing with a simple amino acid called D-serine improved memory and learning, offering a potential new approach to age-related cognitive decline.

articles.title: Just 10 minutes of daily exercise could unlock deeper sleep
articles.summary: Getting better sleep might be as simple as moving a little more every day. Researchers at The University of Texas at Austin found that people who exercised more frequently experienced more deep, restorative sleep, which is essential for brain recovery, memory, and emotional well-being. Surprisingly, just 10 minutes of moderate to vigorous exercise per day was associated with measurable benefits, while even light activities like walking and standing breaks were linked to better sleep and mood.

articles.title: The hidden math of Alzheimer's could point to new treatments
articles.summary: Mathematics may hold unexpected clues to understanding Alzheimer’s disease. Scientists have developed a model showing how common metals like copper and zinc may influence the buildup of proteins associated with the disease, while also exploring possible ways to stop the process. The findings could help researchers identify promising strategies for preventing harmful plaque formation.

articles.title: Scientists created a tiny device that can control your nerves to treat chronic pain
articles.summary: Scientists have developed a tiny, injectable device that can control nerve activity without surgery, batteries, or wires, potentially transforming treatment for chronic pain and movement disorders. Powered wirelessly from outside the body, the seed-sized technology has shown promising results in early testing.

articles.title: Algebraic Integer Quantization for Machine Learning Applications
articles.summary: arXiv:2610.12494v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this article, we propose algebraic integer number formats (AINF) as a framework for highly configurable and accurate compressed computation. A key property of AINF is its straightforward reduction to purely integer arithmetic, enabling error-free multiply-accumulate operations. We develop a matrix multiplication engine that exploits this property, obtaining performance within a predictable factor of the most efficient numerical counterparts on modern hardware accelerators.
